complexity.engineConfigNotCode: Once the engine exists, variants, bundles and regional prices become rows of configuration; the next pricing request ships without a deploy.
complexity.engineAccidental: A rule language, its evaluator, precedence and an admin screen are complexity the business never asked for. Three real cases did not need a general solution.
complexity.engineBuildTime: Building the engine takes about two of five engineers for most of the quarter.
complexity.engineRuleCollisions: Within a quarter, two rules match the same product and the cheaper one wins by accident. Wrong prices reach real checkouts before anyone notices.
complexity.engineNobodyReadsRules: Six months on, the rules table is the real pricing code, and nobody can say what a given product will cost without running it.
complexity.engineHiresLearnDsl: After the seed round, every new hire has to learn an in-house rule language that exists nowhere else and has no debugger.
complexity.catalogSlowerNow: Modelling variants, bundles and regional prices explicitly takes most of the quarter; sellers wait about six weeks longer than with a SaaS.
complexity.catalogEssentialOnly: Three cases written as three cases add only the complexity the problem already had.
complexity.catalogEngineeringTime: The quarter spent on the module is roughly the same salary spent as the engine; it just buys less flexibility.
complexity.catalogDeepInterface: One small interface (price this cart for this region) hides three cases; callers learn one call, not three models.
complexity.catalogCasesTested: Explicit cases are easy to test one by one; pricing regressions drop within a quarter.
complexity.catalogCheapToChange: Because the cases are named in code, changing one of them is a local edit. Two quarters on, pricing changes are faster than in either alternative.
complexity.catalogFourthCase: With seed money comes a sales team, and sales promises a fourth case (wholesale tiers) that the module does not have yet. Someone has to write it.
complexity.saasShipsNow: A catalog SaaS supports variants and bundles out of the box; integration is a few weeks, not a quarter.
complexity.saasSubscription: The subscription is priced per SKU and per seat; at a few hundred orders a day it is a visible line on the bill.
complexity.saasAnnualContract: The vendor wants the first year paid up front, about a month of runway.
complexity.saasTheirModel: The team stops owning the catalog model; sellers configure products in the vendor's screens, not in tickets to engineering.
complexity.saasGlueAndLockIn: Sync jobs, webhooks and a translation layer between their product model and your orders. Every month of data in their format makes leaving more expensive.
complexity.saasStalePrices: Prices live in two places. Within a quarter, a webhook is missed and a seller's new price shows in the vendor's screen but not at checkout.
complexity.saasPriceChange: When the vendor reprices, a commodity becomes a negotiation you have no leverage in: the bill rises and migrating costs more than paying.
complexity.seedRunway: The seed round closes and adds about eighteen months of runway at the current burn.
complexity.saasBlackFridayLimits: The catalog vendor rate-limits at peak; product pages degrade exactly when traffic is highest.
complexity.engineKeyEngineer: The in-house rule language was tacit knowledge; the person who leaves took the grammar with them.

complexity.title: Sellers want variants, bundles and regional prices
complexity.concept: Essential vs accidental complexity, and the real price of each abstraction.
complexity.voice: Every abstraction is a loan. Some come with a fair rate.
complexity.briefing: Q3 of Year 1. Five engineers, a few hundred orders a day, and a stack of seller requests: sizes and colours, three-for-two bundles, a different price in Monterrey. The problem has three real cases. How many the solution has is up to you.
complexity.dilemma: How much of this complexity belongs to the problem, and how much are you about to add?
complexity.disagreement: Experts disagree here. Some say three cases are the moment to generalise, before the fourth arrives; others say the right abstraction only shows itself after the cases, and a deep module beats a flexible one. Brooks would ask which part is essence and which part is yours.
complexity.readNext: Read Brooks on essence and accident, then Ousterhout's chapter on deep modules, then place your catalog on a Wardley map and ask whether it has become a commodity.

pricing-engine.title: A configurable pricing and rules engine
pricing-engine.optimizes: Any future pricing idea becomes configuration, and sellers stop waiting for a deploy.
pricing-engine.costs: A rule language someone has to design, test and document; if the rules grow without an owner, in six months nobody can read them.

catalog-module.title: Model the three cases in a deep catalog module
catalog-module.optimizes: Only the essential complexity; cheap to change once it exists.
catalog-module.costs: Most of the quarter; sellers wait, and the fourth case is code, not config.

catalog-saas.title: Buy a catalog SaaS (PIM)
catalog-saas.optimizes: Variants and bundles this month, built by someone else.
catalog-saas.costs: A subscription, prices living in two places, and a data model that is theirs.

events.seed-round: Monday, 09:00. The seed round has closed. Eighteen more months, and a board that would like to see them used.

inspections.three-ways-to-price: Site inspection: asked which price a bundle gets in Monterrey, three engineers gave two answers. Not a bug yet. A question, written in the margin.

review.essential-or-accidental: Which part of what you built is essential to selling things, and which part did you add?
review.who-pays-later: What did you give up, and who pays for it a year from now?
review.when-revisit: What would make you revisit this, and how would you know?

rubric.grounded-context: The context names the constraints that actually shaped the choice (team, orders, runway, seller requests).
rubric.names-essence: The decision separates the problem's own complexity from the complexity the solution adds.
rubric.names-tradeoff: The consequences name at least one force that got worse, not only the ones that got better.
rubric.names-given-up: What was given up is written down in a full sentence.
rubric.revisit-trigger: The revisit trigger is a condition someone could notice, not a hope.
